children.value: The Adverse Childhood Experiences questionnaire (ACE) is not part of the core questions of this study. It was included to give a first, broad view of which aspects of structural inference could be worth focusing on in planned studies of structural inference after childhood adversity. The ACE is a coarse instrument (ten yes/no items on abuse, neglect and household dysfunction before age 18) compared with the MACE or the CTQ, which record type, timing and severity.

This chapter runs the questionnaire-dependent analyses of the study with the ACE total score as the only score. All numbers refer to run 23_11 (96 participants, 95 with ACE scores; pupil data for 84 of them, gaze data for 86). Slopes are per SD of the ACE score. Because the ACE correlates with current symptoms (section 1), every participant-level effect is also reported with the general questionnaire factor (
) and its interaction with condition as covariates.

children.value: ACE total: median 1 (IQR 0–2), mean 1.37 (SD 1.51), range 0–6; 36 participants report no adverse experience and 8 report four or more. Abuse and neglect: mean 0.66 (SD 1.00); household dysfunction: mean 0.71 (SD 0.89). The conditions do not differ (Kruskal–Wallis H = 1.83, p = .40; None 1.49 ± 1.76, n = 37; Partial 1.47 ± 1.36, n = 36; Full 1.00 ± 1.27, n = 22).
ACE total correlates with the current symptom scores (Spearman, n = 95): general factor ρ = .38, STICSA trait .37, STICSA state .34, OCI .33, BDI-II .28, IUS .27 (all p < .01).

Of the 64 participant-level measures, five have an across-condition slope with p < .05 without and five with the general factor; after correction within module, the Nexus switch probability (both models) and the pupil–surprise slope of the n-state model (without the general factor) remain at q < .05.

Placement error (A1): ACE slope p = .105, across conditions p = .17; interception (A2): p = .64. Transition-versus-oddball response (B1, error; event × trial × ACE): across conditions p = .084, condition dependence p = .13; net entropy (B2): event × trial × ACE p = .091 (cluster-robust CR2 p = .041), across conditions p = .11. Weighting of state error (C): the additional weight on state error increases with ACE (se × ACE F = 6.18, p = .013; slope per SD 0.082 in None, 0.059 in Partial, 0.100 in Full; condition dependence p = .31); with cluster-robust standard errors p = .26, and in the sensitivity model with random slopes p = .11. Transfer to the second cue (D): |I_e| increases by 5.1° per SD across conditions (p = .071; CR2 p = .053).

The share of split placements at t+2 after transitions increases with ACE (0.27 SD per SD, p = .008, q = .10; Spearman on the condition residuals ρ = .21, p = .043), with similar slopes in the three conditions (None 0.24, Partial 0.38, Full 0.18; all differences p > .50). The slope is unchanged with the general factor (0.29, p = .010). The entropy decomposition of the nets after events gives the same direction: the probability that the nets are split over two clusters increases with ACE at t+1 after oddballs (0.59 log-odds per SD, p = .035) and at t+2 after oddballs (0.56, p = .048) and after transitions (0.57, p = .053). Both ACE subscales show the split-placement slope (abuse and neglect 0.27, p = .010; household dysfunction 0.17, p = .090).

Among the structure models, one term relates to ACE: in the model of following the new position at t+1 (S5), the change from the first to the second half of the session in the transition-minus-oddball difference depends on ACE (event × half × ACE −0.83 log-odds per SD, SE 0.24, p < .001). The other structure terms (oddball type, alternative directions, temporal structure, commitment, correctness at t+2) have p > .10. Shifts after transitions and oddballs, switching and following at t+1, net entropy, the stable-trial distance, replayed uncertainty and placement duration, the change of the stable-trial distance over the session and the cue transfer gap do not relate to ACE (participant level, all p > .10). The colour-cue learning measures do not relate to ACE (all p > .09).
The switch probability h_switch increases with ACE (

): RQ3 model with plausible values 0.33 SD per SD (SE 0.11, p = .004; F = 9.23, q = .003), in the latent-state sample F = 8.62, p = .004. Within conditions (participant level) 0.29 in None (p = .037), 0.25 in Partial (p = .27) and 0.46 in Full (p = .003); the conditions do not differ (all p > .40). With the general factor the slope is 0.37 (p < .001, q = .002); Spearman on the condition residuals ρ = .22 (p = .029). The slope is carried mainly by abuse and neglect (0.29, p = .004) and less by household dysfunction (0.20, p = .084). The action-rule variant lam gives the same result for h_switch (0.36, p = .001; Full 0.68, p = .004) and a positive noise-reactivity slope in Full (0.49, p = .047). The other five Nexus parameters do not relate to ACE (all p > .10).

No parameter of the change-point observer or of the n-state model relates to ACE (RQ3 models: all p > .08; smallest p for the n-state precision weighting, F = 3.04, p = .085).
Noise sensitivity v, the probability of four states and the reliance on the structure w do not relate to ACE (across conditions all p > .44; within conditions all p > .30).

The advantage of the n-state model over simple tracking increases with ACE across conditions (0.21 SD per SD, p = .044; HC3 p = .081); the advantage of Nexus over simple tracking and over the change-point observer increases with ACE in Full (0.57, p = .030 and 0.56, p = .032) but not in None and Partial.

The participant slopes of the feedback pupil on model surprise (controlled for the model-free prediction error) increase with ACE for all three models, most clearly for the n-state model: 0.35 SD per SD (p = .003, q = .028; ρ = .28, p = .010), 0.32 with the general factor (p = .008). For Nexus (0.27, p = .083) and the change-point observer (0.25, p = .043) the slopes are carried by None (0.55, p = .069 and 0.49, p = .004) and are halved by the general factor (0.13, p = .24 and 0.13, p = .22). The n-state slope is carried by household dysfunction (0.34, p = .001) more than by abuse and neglect (0.20, p = .22). The coupling of the feedback pupil with the Nexus belief update, the baseline pupil, the coupling of the baseline pupil and of the pupil before the outcome with replayed uncertainty, and the pupil difference between bites and blocked attacks do not relate to ACE (all p > .25).

Gaze: location entropy, the share at the third location and the share beyond the task locations in the prediction and anticipation windows do not relate to ACE (across conditions all p > .11; with the general factor all p > .09). Mouse tracking: placement entropy, curvature, direction changes of the first movement, the number of nets and the time to the first net do not relate to ACE (all p > .15).

The trial-level models of the six in-task ratings have no ACE term with p < .10. At the participant level, mean in-task anxiety, stress, valence, arousal and fatigue do not relate to ACE (all p > .18); with the general factor, stress is lower with higher ACE (−0.21 SD per SD, p = .050). Participants with higher ACE rate the instructions as clearer (0.19, p = .022; mostly in Partial, 0.39, p = .069). The change of aversiveness over the session and noticing the rule do not relate to ACE.

ACE total relates to three aspects of structural inference, each robust to the general factor: a higher switch probability in the Nexus model (in all conditions), more split placements after transitions (nets on both the old and the new direction), and a stronger coupling of the feedback pupil with the surprise of the n-state model. The ACE does not relate to accuracy, to the other model parameters, to the hybrid model, to gaze and cursor measures or to in-task affect. For a study of structural inference after childhood adversity, these results point to the belief about how often the hidden state changes and to the hedging between states after a change as candidate targets, with the abuse and neglect items carrying the switch-probability effect.
